author: Grace Chen
title: AMA & Black Doctors: Racism Revealed | Tufts Research
text:
The “Colored” Designation: How the AMA Systematically Discriminated Against Black Physicians
A century ago, the American medical Association (AMA) actively worked to marginalize Black doctors, a practice that continues to contribute to racial disparities in healthcare today.New research reveals the extent of this discrimination, detailing how the AMA labeled Black physicians in its directories – a practice that lasted for over three decades and actively hindered their professional advancement.
Before the Civil War, Black Americans seeking medical degrees faced notable hurdles, often requiring education abroad. The post-Civil War era saw the founding of numerous Black medical schools between 1868 and 1904, considerably increasing the number of Black medical graduates.However,institutions like University Medical School,Meharry Medical College,and Leonard Medical School faced an uphill battle as the AMA systematically excluded Black physicians from membership and official listings.
By 1906, the AMA’s records showed that only 1.8% of all physicians in the United States were African American. What’s more, the AMA explicitly identified these doctors in its directories with the label “Col” – short for “Colored” – effectively segregating them within the profession.According to Benjamin Chrisinger, an assistant professor in Tufts University’s Department of community Health, this practice was deeply opposed by Black medical leaders at the time. “It contributed to the further exclusion of black physicians from medical training, practice, and professional communities,” Chrisinger explained.
chrisinger’s research, titled “Deep Roots of Racial Inequalities in US Healthcare: The 1906 American Medical Directory,” analyzes digitized past records from the AMA’s 1906 directory, offering a stark look at the history of medical discrimination and illuminating the persistent gap between Black doctors and the Black population. The AMA began labeling Black physicians in its directories in 1906, continuing the practice until 1938. “The National Medical Association opposed it from the start, so we certainly know that this wasn’t something that Black doctors were volunteering,” Chrisinger stated. “The AMA was forcing this kind of distinction.”
The directory wasn’t an isolated incident,but rather part of a broader effort by the AMA to establish itself as the ultimate authority on qualified medical professionals. Historian Vanessa northington Gamble of George Washington University discovered correspondence revealing that AMA officials actively inquired about the race of medical school graduates with secretaries,archive staff,and medical school presidents. As Chrisinger noted, “There’s no checkbox for it, so doctors weren’t asked to give that information directly, but somehow, the data was still being gathered.”
In 1906, Chrisinger’s analysis revealed there were 746 Black doctors practicing in 16 states, with 57% having received their education at Howard or Meharry. His investigation began after reading the AMA’s 2008 apology for its history of discriminatory practices against Black physicians, prompting him to examine the structures that perpetuate health disparities. Chrisinger’s work focuses on how the AMA’s labeling practices coincided with its attempts to “professionalize” and “standardize” medicine, and to exert greater control over medical education.
The research also highlights the multifaceted role Black doctors played in their communities. They weren’t simply healthcare providers, but also economic anchors, frequently owning real estate, operating local businesses, and providing informal loans
